title: The Bitter Broccoli
twist: The obvious answer — 'she's just a picky eater' — is wrong. Her tongue really is detecting a bitter chemical more strongly than her brother's, and she inherited that.
briefing: Imani, 13, pushes her broccoli around the plate every time it's served. She says it tastes harshly bitter, almost like medicine. Her brother eats the same broccoli and says it's mild and fine.
question: Is Imani just being picky — or is something different about how she tastes?

clues.title: Refuses the broccoli
clues.text: She won't eat broccoli or Brussels sprouts. But she happily eats carrots, corn and peppers, and says the green ones taste 'sharp and bitter'.
clues.shows: a strong bitter taste from only certain vegetables

clues.title: Brother shrugs
clues.text: Same pan, same dinner: her brother says the broccoli is barely bitter at all. He can't see what the fuss is about.
clues.shows: the same food tasting different to two people

clues.title: The paper-strip test
clues.text: In science class everyone tastes a paper strip with a harmless bitter chemical on it. Imani pulls a face; her brother, at home, says his tastes of nothing but paper.
clues.shows: her tongue detecting a bitter chemical that others barely notice

clues.title: Runs in the family
clues.text: Her mom also can't stand Brussels sprouts, and so could her grandma. Her dad loves them, just like her brother.

hypotheses.flaw: A picky eater turns down lots of foods; Imani likes most vegetables and only rejects the bitter ones — and a paper strip doesn't care about attitude.
Her brother ate the same broccoli and found it mild, and the paper strip had nothing to do with cooking.

hypotheses.text: Imani inherited extra-sensitive bitter-taste receptors on her tongue, so the same chemical in broccoli tastes much more bitter to her than to her brother.
She has a cold and can't taste properly.
hypotheses.flaw: A cold makes food taste of less, not more — Imani is tasting more bitterness than everyone else.

prediction.prompt: As food gets more bitter — from cucumber to broccoli to raw Brussels sprouts — how bitter does it taste to Imani?

second.question: Compared with her brother, does the same broccoli taste more or less bitter to Imani?

transfer.context: Raj and his best friend share the same cup of black hot chocolate made with dark cocoa. Raj says it's harshly bitter; his friend says it just tastes rich.
options: The hot chocolate was made too strong.
Raj is pretending, to make his friend laugh.
Raj probably inherited more sensitive bitter-taste receptors, so the same chemicals taste stronger to him.
transfer.retryHint: Same cup, two people, two different tastes — which of Imani's clues showed exactly that?
transfer.explanation: They drank from the same cup, so the drink can't be the difference. Like Imani, Raj's tongue likely carries more sensitive bitter receptors — something people inherit — so the same chemicals in dark cocoa send him a much stronger bitter signal.

takeaway: Taste isn't the same for everyone. Genes help decide how sensitive your bitter-taste receptors are, so the same broccoli can be mild to one person and harsh to another — that's biology, not pickiness.
